title: Funding cuts, the Lisp machine collapse, second winter
text:
CHAPTER 11. THE AI WINTERS
SECTION 11.2. FUNDING CUTS, THE LISP MACHINE COLLAPSE AND THE SECOND WINTER

The first AI winter (Section 11.1) ended in the early 1980s with a boom built on a narrower, more practical idea: expert systems that captured the knowledge of human specialists in rules (Chapter 12 explains how they work). Governments and corporations invested heavily. By the end of the decade the boom had turned to bust: the specialized hardware market collapsed, government programs missed their goals, and expert systems proved costly and brittle. This second winter, roughly from 1987 into the 1990s, had economic causes as much as scientific ones. Understanding it is useful for anyone who builds technology products, because the same forces (hardware commoditization, maintenance costs, inflated expectations) operate today.

1. The boom of the early 1980s

Several developments drove a renewed wave of enthusiasm.

Commercial expert systems. The first commercially successful expert system was XCON (originally R1), developed at Carnegie Mellon University for Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC), from 1978 by John McDermott, written in the OPS5 rule language, and in use at DEC from 1980. It configured VAX computer orders: given a customer's order, it determined which components, cables and cabinets were needed and how to arrange them. XCON was estimated to have saved DEC on the order of 40 million dollars over six years, according to commonly cited figures. Other companies followed, and by 1985 corporations were spending over a billion dollars a year on AI, much of it in in-house AI groups. An industry grew up around the tools: software firms such as Teknowledge and IntelliCorp (with its KEE knowledge engineering environment), and hardware firms selling Lisp machines.

Japan's Fifth Generation project. In 1981-1982 Japan's Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) launched the Fifth Generation Computer Systems project (FGCS), a 10-year initiative run through a dedicated institute (ICOT). Its aim was to build massively parallel computers for AI applications based on concurrent logic programming (a parallel descendant of Prolog), with goals that included conversation, translation, image interpretation and reasoning over large knowledge bases. MITI reportedly set aside about 850 million dollars for it. In the West, the project was widely seen as a challenge, at a time when Japanese industry was overtaking American and European firms in electronics and cars.

Responses to Japan:

  - United Kingdom: the Alvey programme, starting in 1983, funded information technology research, including AI, with a budget of about 350 million pounds, partly reversing the cuts after the Lighthill report.
  - United States: DARPA launched the Strategic Computing Initiative (SCI) in 1983, a large program aiming at machine intelligence for military applications, including an autonomous land vehicle, a pilot's associate for fighter aircraft, and battle management systems. The US also formed the Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation (MCC), an industry research consortium.
  - Europe: the ESPRIT program funded collaborative IT research.

The neural network revival. In parallel, neural networks came back: Hopfield networks (1982), and backpropagation popularized in 1986 by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams (Chapter 13). This part of the field would grow through the second winter rather than be destroyed by it.

2. Warnings

In 1984, at the annual meeting of the American Association for Artificial Intelligence (AAAI), Roger Schank and Marvin Minsky, who had lived through the 1970s cuts, warned the business community that enthusiasm for AI had spiraled out of control and that disappointment would follow. The term "AI winter" appeared at that 1984 debate, by analogy with "nuclear winter," a chain reaction of pessimism: first in the research community, then the press, then funding cuts, then the end of serious research. Three years later, events seemed to confirm the warning.

3. The Lisp machine collapse (1987)

Lisp machines (Section 9.2) were workstations whose hardware and microcode were optimized for Lisp: tagged memory for type checking, hardware support for garbage collection, microcoded function calls. They were made by Symbolics (the 3600 series), Lisp Machines Inc. (LMI), Texas Instruments (the Explorer) and Xerox. In the early 1980s they offered the best environment for large AI programs, with excellent development tools, and they sold for prices typically in the tens of thousands of dollars or more per seat.

Then general-purpose hardware caught up. Workstations from companies such as Sun Microsystems, based on commodity microprocessors (the Motorola 68000 family, then RISC chips like SPARC; Section 6.4), improved rapidly, and companies such as Lucid and Franz offered high-quality Common Lisp implementations for them. Apple and IBM desktop machines also became capable of running Lisp and expert system shells. By 1987 some of these machines had become as powerful as the more expensive Lisp machines. In 1987 the market for specialized Lisp hardware collapsed: in a frequently quoted phrase from Crevier's history, an entire industry worth half a billion dollars was replaced in a single year. LMI went bankrupt in 1987; Symbolics struggled for years and declined; TI and Xerox left the market.

The engineering lesson is general. A specialized architecture gives an advantage of a constant factor (say, a few times faster on its target workload). A general-purpose platform with a much larger market improves exponentially and gains economies of scale. Unless the specialized platform keeps a large advantage and improves as fast, the general platform overtakes it. This has happened repeatedly: Lisp machines, many parallel supercomputer startups of the late 1980s and 1990s (Thinking Machines, for example), and dedicated hardware for various tasks. The current exception, GPUs and AI accelerators (Chapter 15), succeeded because the workload (dense matrix arithmetic) became enormous, the speedups are very large (often 10-100 times or more), and the market for them became large enough to fund rapid improvement themselves.

4. The problems with expert systems

Expert systems delivered real value in narrow tasks, but they ran into limits that became obvious as companies tried to scale them:

  - Knowledge acquisition bottleneck: extracting rules from experts was slow, expensive and incomplete; experts often cannot articulate what they know.
  - Maintenance: large rule bases became hard to update. Adding a rule could interact unexpectedly with hundreds of others. XCON grew to thousands of rules (about 2,500 in one commonly cited count; other sources give larger figures for later versions) and required a substantial team to maintain; by the early 1990s, early successful systems such as XCON were proving too expensive to maintain.
  - Brittleness: systems could make absurd mistakes on inputs slightly outside what their rules anticipated, with no awareness that they were out of their depth.
  - No learning: they did not improve from experience.
  - The qualification problem: real rules have endless exceptions ("a bird can fly unless it is a penguin, an ostrich, injured, dead, in a cage..."), a problem studied in nonmonotonic logic, and not solvable simply by adding rules.

These limits made expert systems useful but not the revolution that marketing had suggested. Many companies quietly folded their AI groups or relabeled the technology. Rule-based systems did not disappear: they live on as "business rules engines," configuration systems, diagnostic tools and in parts of industrial control (Chapter 12). But "AI" as a product label became something to avoid.

5. Government programs end

Strategic Computing. In 1987 Jack Schwarz became head of DARPA's Information Processing Techniques Office (IPTO). He was skeptical of AI, dismissed expert systems as "clever programming," and cut AI funding sharply; in his words DARPA should "surf" (fund technologies already showing great promise) rather than "dog paddle." By the early 1990s, SCI's ambitious goals had not been met. The autonomous land vehicle and the pilot's associate were not delivered as originally envisioned. One SCI-related success is often noted: the DART logistics planning tool (Dynamic Analysis and Replanning Tool), used in the 1990-1991 Gulf War, which was credited with saving very large sums in logistics, by some accounts more than DARPA's entire previous investment in AI.

Fifth Generation. FGCS ran from 1982 to 1992. It produced parallel inference machines and research results in concurrent logic programming, and trained many researchers, but its headline goals (machines that converse and reason like people) were far from met. By 1991 its list of goals from 1981 had not been met. The parallel logic machines were overtaken by fast commodity microprocessors, the same dynamic that defeated Lisp machines. In HP Newquist's account, the project ended on June 1, 1992 "not with a successful roar, but with a whimper." Logic programming did not become the foundation of computing.

Alvey also wound down, losing its second-phase funding.

6. Dating and depth of the second winter

Sources date the second winter differently: some say 1987-1993, others extend it toward 2000. Commercial AI as a label was unpopular through the 1990s. Researchers often described their work as "machine learning," "knowledge-based systems," "informatics," "computational intelligence" or "pattern recognition" to avoid the stigma.

But the 1990s were also a decade of rapid scientific progress under these other names:

  - Statistical methods: hidden Markov models in speech recognition, statistical machine translation, Bayesian networks (Judea Pearl, 1988), support vector machines and kernel methods (Chapter 14).
  - Reinforcement learning: temporal-difference learning, Q-learning (Watkins, 1989), and TD-Gammon (Tesauro, early 1990s), a backgammon program that learned to play at expert level.
  - Neural networks in applications: LeCun's convolutional networks for handwritten digit recognition, used commercially in reading checks in the 1990s (Chapter 16).
  - Search and game playing: Deep Blue's 1997 victory over Kasparov (Section 8.3).
  - Robotics: probabilistic robotics (Kalman and particle filters for localization and mapping) made mobile robots reliable.

What changed was the style of AI: away from hand-written knowledge and toward probability, statistics, optimization and learning from data, with careful empirical evaluation. That shift set up the machine learning era (Chapters 14-16).

7. The cycle

The two winters show a pattern often compared to the Gartner "hype cycle": a technology trigger, a peak of inflated expectations, a trough of disillusionment, then a slope of enlightenment and a plateau of productivity. AI followed it twice:

    first cycle:  1956 Dartmouth -> 1960s optimism -> 1966 ALPAC,
                  1969 Mansfield, 1973 Lighthill -> 1974-1980 winter
    second cycle: 1980 XCON, 1982 FGCS, 1983 SCI -> 1987 Lisp machine
                  collapse, 1987 DARPA cuts, 1992 FGCS end -> winter

Some common factors:

  - Demonstrations on narrow problems were taken as evidence for broad capabilities.
  - Scaling was harder than expected (search explosion in the first cycle, knowledge acquisition and maintenance in the second).
  - Funders and companies made decisions based on expected timelines that were too short.
  - Specialized hardware was overtaken by commodity hardware.
  - The research did not stop; it changed names and methods.

8. A 2026 perspective

The current AI boom, driven by deep learning and large language models (Chapters 16-19), differs from earlier ones in important ways: products are used by hundreds of millions of people, revenues are real, and capabilities improve measurably with scale. It also shares some features: very large capital investment (in data centers and accelerators) based on expected future returns, predictions of human-level AI within a few years by some leaders, and uncertainty about the costs of reliability, maintenance and integration into real work. Whether a third winter, a gentler correction, or continued growth follows is not something history can settle. What history does suggest is to evaluate systems on realistic tasks, to be careful with extrapolation, to watch the economics of hardware and maintenance, and to remember that a field's long-term progress can survive the collapse of its short-term hype.

9. Summary

  - The early 1980s boom was driven by commercial expert systems (XCON at DEC), Japan's Fifth Generation project (1982-1992), and responses such as Alvey (UK, 1983) and DARPA's Strategic Computing Initiative (1983).
  - In 1984 Schank and Minsky warned at AAAI that an "AI winter" would follow the hype.
  - In 1987 the Lisp machine market collapsed as Sun workstations and PCs running Common Lisp became as fast and much cheaper.
  - Expert systems suffered from the knowledge acquisition bottleneck, maintenance cost, brittleness, lack of learning and the qualification problem.
  - DARPA cut AI funding from 1987 under Jack Schwarz; SCI and FGCS missed their headline goals, though DART was a notable success.
  - In the second winter (about 1987 into the 1990s), the field reorganized around statistics, probability and machine learning, setting up the modern era.
